questions.question: What is GORM and how does it differ from database/sql?
questions.title: Gorm Basics Go
questions.direct_answer: GORM is Go's ORM: structs map to tables (gorm.Model + field tags), AutoMigrate creates tables, and CRUD is method calls (db.First, db.Create, db.Where). It replaces raw SQL with struct operations — at the cost of generated queries and abstraction.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: GORM is Go's ORM: structs map to tables (gorm.Model + field tags), AutoMigrate creates tables, and CRUD is method calls (db.First, db.Create, db.Where). It replaces raw SQL with struct operations — at the cost of generated queries and abstraction.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The model + operations:

```go
type User struct {
    gorm.Model              // ID, CreatedAt, UpdatedAt, DeletedAt — built-in
    Name  string
    Email string `gorm:"uniqueIndex"`
}

// Setup
db, _ := gorm.Open(sqlite.Open("app.db"), &gorm.Config{})
db.AutoMigrate(&User{})   // CREATE TABLE — from the struct

// Create — INSERT
db.Create(&User{Name: "Al", Email: "al@x.com"})

// Read — SELECT
db.First(&user, "name = ?", "Al")          // SELECT * WHERE name = 'Al' LIMIT 1
db.Where("age > ?", 18).Find(&users)       // SELECT * WHERE age > 18

// Update
db.Model(&user).Update("name", "Alice")     // UPDATE users SET name = 'Alice'

// Delete (soft — sets DeletedAt)
db.Delete(&user)                          // UPDATE deleted_at — not actually gone
```

What GORM adds over database/sql:
1. Models — the struct IS the schema (no SQL column mapping in Scan)
2. AutoMigrate — the table appears from the struct (dev convenience; production migrations use a tool)
3. Associations — `db.Preload("Orders")` handles the JOIN, the related structs populated
4. Hooks — BeforeCreate, AfterUpdate — lifecycle callbacks on the model
5. Soft deletes — the DeletedAt field = 'deleted' rows filtered automatically

The honest costs:
- The generated SQL isn't always what you'd write (N+1 without Preload; surprising WHERE clauses)
- The abstraction leaks — you still need to know what SQL it's producing
- Performance-sensitive paths drop to raw (db.Raw(...), db.Exec) — which GORM supports

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S[struct User] --> AM[AutoMigrate] --> T[table users]
    C[db.Create user] --> INSERT
    F[db.First where] → SELECT
    U[db.Model Update] → UPDATE
    D[db.Delete] → SOFT[UPDATE deleted_at]
    PRE[db.Preload Orders] --> IN[one IN query — no N+1]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The N+1 problem, which is GORM's most infamous trap: looping over users and calling user.Orders loads each user's orders with a separate query — 100 users = 101 queries. Preload fixes it (one IN query — db.Preload("Orders").Find(&users)), but only if you know it. The equivalent raw-SQL mistake is fewer levels removed — which is the abstraction trade: GORM makes the wrong path easy.

The GORM vs database/sql decision, which is the interview's real question: database/sql + explicit SQL for query-critical services (full control, no surprise queries, no GORM dependency); GORM for CRUD-heavy internal services (speed of development, the struct-schema binding). The middle path many teams use: GORM for the CRUD scaffolding, raw SQL through GORM's db.Raw for the hot/complex queries.

The migration story: AutoMigrate adds columns but doesn't remove or rename — it's a dev convenience, not a migration tool. Production uses versioned migrations (goose, atlas, golang-migrate) — the discipline GORM doesn't replace.
